headline: Congress directs that a gold medal be awarded to the Monuments Men, who protected and returned cultural artworks during and after World War II.
what_it_does: The law asks the House Speaker and the Senate President pro tempore to arrange a single Congressional Gold Medal honoring the Monuments Men, the men and women of the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives Section who served under the Allied armies in World War II. The medal must be displayed at the Smithsonian Institution. Congress also expresses a wish that it be shown at other places linked to the Monuments Men, with preference for Smithsonian-affiliated locations. The Treasury Secretary may make and sell bronze duplicates, priced to cover the cost of making them.

who_it_affects.group: Surviving and descendant Monuments Men and women
who_it_affects.how: They or their families are the honorees of a national gold medal recognizing their wartime service.
The medal is required to be on display at the Smithsonian, where visitors can see it.

who_it_affects.group: People who want to buy a commemorative replica
who_it_affects.how: The Treasury Secretary may strike bronze duplicates of the medal and sell them at a price that covers costs.

when_it_takes_effect: The law took effect when it was enacted on June 9, 2014.
